title: Deviation in Small-Angle Prism
notes: Small-Angle Prism: A prism with small refracting angle A (typically < 10°). For such prisms, the deviation is small and approximately independent of angle of incidence.
Small Angle Deviation Formula: D ≈ (μ - 1)A where μ is refractive index of prism material and A is prism angle (in radians). Derived from D_min formula using small angle approximations sin θ ≈ θ.
Derivation: At minimum deviation for small angles: sin((A+D)/2) ≈ (A+D)/2 and sin(A/2) ≈ A/2. So μ ≈ ((A+D)/2)/(A/2) = (A+D)/A = 1 + D/A. Therefore D ≈ (μ - 1)A.
Independence from Incidence: For small-angle prisms, deviation is nearly constant for a range of incidence angles — unlike large-angle prisms where D varies significantly with i.
Direct Vision Spectroscope: Uses small-angle crown and flint prisms arranged to produce dispersion without net deviation (direct vision) or deviation without dispersion (achromatic combination).
Applications: Simple spectroscopes, direct vision prisms, small angle deviation measurements in optics.
Limitations: Formula breaks down for large A (> 15-20°) or when angles are not small. Full prism formula must be used.
specificConditions: Small Angle Requirement: A must be small (< 10°) and angles small for sin θ ≈ θ approximation.
Near Minimum Deviation: Formula derived at minimum deviation but approximately valid for nearby incidence angles.
Monochromatic Light: μ depends on wavelength — formula applies to one color at a time.
formulas: Small angle prism formula: μ ≈ 1 + D/A
Full prism formula: μ = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2)
Small angle sin approximation: sin θ ≈ θ (θ in radians)

Valid for A < 10° and small incidence angles.

Statement 2: Deviation is approximately independent of angle of incidence for small-angle prisms.
Statement 3: Formula derived using sin θ ≈ θ small angle approximation.
Statement 4: Valid for prism angle A < 10° approximately.

importantNotes: Convert A to radians if using D = (μ-1)A with dimensional consistency (though degrees work if consistent).
Approximation error grows as A increases — use full formula for precision.
This is why small prisms are used in direct vision spectroscopes — predictable deviation.

examples: Compare: Full formula for A = 5°, D = 2.5°: μ = sin(3.75°)/sin(2.5°) = 0.0654/0.0436 = 1.50 — matches small angle approx.
Large angle A = 60°, D_min = 38°: small angle formula gives D = (1.5-1)×60 = 30° — wrong (actual 38°). Shows approximation breakdown.

universalFacts: Small angle prisms are used in direct vision spectroscopes where the beam direction is unchanged but spectrum is visible.
The approximation sin θ ≈ θ has error < 1% for θ < 10° — justifies small angle prism use.
Amici prisms (direct vision) combine crown and flint glass small prisms for zero net deviation with dispersion.
confusion: Using D = (μ-1)A for large angle prisms: Significant error — only valid for small A.
Thinking deviation is exactly independent of incidence: Only approximately true for small-angle prisms.
